questions.statement: Complete the schedule entry: 'The English exam starts ___ 9:00 ___ Thursday morning.'
questions.context: English class in Soyapango, SV.

options.feedback: That pair swaps the two functions: 'on' goes with days and 'at' belongs with clock times, so it reverses the correct order.
Use 'at' with a precise clock time and 'on' with a named day, so the exam starts at 9:00 on Thursday.
'In' introduces longer periods such as months and years, so it cannot mark the exact hour 9:00.
'At' fits the hour, but a named day such as Thursday needs 'on' rather than 'in'.

questions.explanation: English pairs 'at' with clock times and 'on' with named days, so a schedule entry reads at 9:00 on Thursday morning and neither slot takes the other preposition.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Ana joined the school photography club in 2021 and is still a member today. Which preposition marks that starting point?
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'For' introduces a length of time, such as five years, and not the year in which an activity began.
'Since' links a past starting point with a situation that is still true in the present, which is exactly Ana's case.
'During 2021' places the membership inside that year without saying anything about the present.
'Until' marks an endpoint in time, the opposite role from the beginning the sentence describes.

questions.explanation: 'Since' introduces the point where an action began when that action reaches into the present, usually with the present perfect, as in 'she has been a member since 2021'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A student writes: 'I have lived in this city in 2019.' Which correction does the sentence need?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.feedback: 'Until 2019' would mark an endpoint, but the student is still living in the city now.
'During 2019' confines the action to that year and says nothing about the present.
'Since 2019' states the starting point of a situation that continues to the present, which fits an ongoing residence.
'For 2019' would need a duration, and a single year that opens an ongoing action is expressed with 'since'.

questions.explanation: With the present perfect the starting point of an ongoing situation takes 'since'; 'in 2019' would place the whole life inside a closed year.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which phrase places an event correctly inside a calendar year?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.feedback: 'On' goes with days and dates, and not with a year taken as a whole period of time.
'At' is reserved for precise clock times, and a year is a span rather than an instant of the day.
Years and months are introduced by 'in', so 'in 2024' is the correct frame for an event inside that year.
'For' expresses a duration the speaker measures, and not the calendar slot where an event sits.

questions.explanation: English uses 'in' for months and years, 'on' for days and dates, and 'at' for clock times, so an event placed inside a year takes 'in'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: We waited ___ the bus for forty minutes. Which preposition completes the sentence?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.feedback: 'For' expresses the duration of a period, and forty minutes is a length of time rather than a point.
'Since' would mark the moment the waiting began, and the sentence measures how long the wait lasted.
'During' needs the name of a period or event, such as 'during the delay' or 'during the storm'.
'At' introduces a point in time, so it would fit 'at six o'clock' and not a span of forty minutes.

questions.explanation: 'For' reports how long something lasts, so a wait of forty minutes takes 'for' rather than a point such as 'at' or a named period such as 'during'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The workshop ends at 4 p.m. Complete the sentence: 'It finishes ___ 4 p.m. ___ the main hall.'
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: The pair is reversed: the clock time takes 'at' and the enclosed place takes 'in'.
'On' would go with a surface such as 'on the stage', and 'at' cannot introduce the main hall.
'At' fits the hour, and an enclosed room or building is introduced by 'in', so this pair works.
'By' marks a deadline rather than the moment an event takes place, so it does not fit the schedule.

questions.explanation: Clock times take 'at' and enclosed places take 'in', which is why the workshop finishes at 4 p.m. in the main hall instead of on it or by it.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The train leaves ___ 6:15 ___ platform three. Which pair of prepositions is correct?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.feedback: That reverses both roles: the hour is not introduced by 'on' and the platform is not introduced by 'at'.
'For' measures a length of time, and 6:15 is a point in the day rather than a duration.
A departure hour takes 'at' and a numbered platform behaves like a surface, so 'on' is the right preposition.
'In' introduces longer periods and enclosed spaces, so it fits neither a precise hour nor a platform.

questions.explanation: Precise hours take 'at' and platforms behave like surfaces that take 'on', which is why the train leaves at 6:15 on platform three.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence places the sports day correctly in time?
questions.context: English class in Soyapango, SV.

options.text: The sports day is on next Friday.
options.feedback: Time expressions built with 'next' normally stand without a preposition, so 'on' is extra here.

options.text: The sports day is in next Friday.
options.feedback: 'In' introduces months and years, and it cannot go with a day such as Friday.

options.text: The sports day is at next Friday.
options.feedback: 'At' belongs with clock times, not with a named weekday such as Friday.

options.text: The sports day is next Friday.
options.feedback: Time expressions such as 'next Friday' normally appear with no time preposition at all.

questions.explanation: Expressions such as 'next Friday', 'last month' and 'every day' normally appear without a preposition, so adding 'on', 'in' or 'at' is a common error.

questions.statement: A shop opens ___ 8 a.m. ___ weekdays. Which pair of prepositions is correct?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.feedback: 'At' marks a single instant, and 'in' takes months, so neither slot fits here.
'For' would need a measured duration, and 'on' cannot introduce a plural such as 'weekdays'.
'In' introduces a month or a year, and 'at' cannot introduce the plural 'weekdays'.
A repeated daily time takes 'at' and 'weekdays' behaves as a named day, so 'on' is right.

questions.explanation: A daily opening hour takes 'at', and 'weekdays' functions as a named day, so the shop opens at 8 a.m. on weekdays rather than in or for them.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The notice says: 'The library is open ___ 8 a.m. ___ Saturdays only.' Which preposition pair fits?
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.feedback: 'At' marks a single instant and 'in' takes months, so neither slot fits an opening hour and a weekday.
'From' opens an interval of time and 'on' introduces a named day, which is exactly what the notice states.
'For' would need a duration and 'in' belongs with a month, so the pair fails on both counts.
'Since' marks a starting point in an ongoing situation and 'at' cannot introduce a named day.

questions.explanation: 'From' introduces the beginning of a time interval and 'on' introduces named days, so the notice reads from 8 a.m. on Saturdays only.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The report is due ___ Friday evening. Which preposition marks the deadline?
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Until' marks the endpoint of a continuing activity, and here the point is when the report must arrive.
'Since' links a past starting point to a situation that still holds, which a deadline does not do.
'By' names the latest moment by which the action must be completed, which is what a due date sets.
'For' reports a length of time the speaker measures, and Friday evening is a point rather than a length.

questions.explanation: 'By' states a deadline, the latest acceptable moment, so a report due Friday evening is submitted by then; 'at' would only locate the submission in time.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence uses 'in' correctly with a period of time?
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.feedback: A named month is a period of time, and periods take 'in' rather than 'on'.
'At' belongs with clock times, and July names a month rather than an instant.
'For' measures a length of time, so it would need 'for two weeks' rather than a month.
Months are introduced by 'in', so this sentence places the course correctly in time.

questions.explanation: 'In' introduces months, years and other closed periods, so a course that runs in July is placed correctly, unlike the same sentence with 'on' or 'at'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A shop assistant says: 'This discount ends ___ Sunday, so buy it before then.' Which preposition is correct?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.feedback: A named day is introduced by 'on', and Sunday is the day on which the discount ends.
'In' introduces months and years, so it cannot go with a single day such as Sunday.
'At' belongs with precise clock times, and Sunday is a calendar day rather than an instant.
'During' needs a period or an event, and 'Sunday' names a single day rather than a span.

questions.explanation: Named days take 'on', so an offer that finishes on Sunday is introduced by 'on', while 'in' takes months and 'at' takes clock times.

questions.statement: Which sentence uses a time preposition correctly?

options.feedback: A precise calendar date is introduced by 'on' in standard use, so 'in' is the wrong choice here.
A precise calendar date is introduced by 'on', so this sentence places the exam correctly.
'At' is reserved for clock times, and a calendar date is not an instant of the day.
'For' reports a duration the speaker measures, and not the day on which an event takes place.

questions.explanation: Clock times take 'at', days and dates take 'on', and months or years take 'in', so a precise date such as 10 May is introduced by 'on'.

questions.statement: Which sentence places the holiday correctly in time?

options.text: Our holiday starts in next July.

An expression such as 'next July' normally appears with no preposition, so this is the correct form.

options.feedback: 'On' goes with a day or a date, and July is a month, so the pair does not match.

options.feedback: 'At' is reserved for precise clock times, and it cannot introduce a month such as July.

questions.statement: The class runs ___ 7 a.m. ___ 8 a.m. How should the interval be expressed?
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'From' opens the interval and 'to' gives its endpoint, so the two halves of the class are placed correctly.
'At' marks a single instant and 'in' takes months or years, so the pair cannot name the two ends of one interval.
Both prepositions describe an ongoing situation, and neither one opens a scheduled interval that ends at 8 a.m.
'For' would need a measured length of time, and it cannot be followed by 'to' to close the interval.

questions.explanation: 'From ... to ...' is the standard frame for an interval with a clear beginning and endpoint, so a class from 7 a.m. to 8 a.m. is expressed that way.

questions.statement: A poster announces: 'Concert ___ Saturday 15 March, at 8 p.m.' Which preposition introduces the date?
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'In' introduces a month or a year on its own, so it cannot carry the full day, month and year of a date.
A calendar date is introduced by 'on', which is why the poster reads 'on Saturday 15 March'.
'At' introduces a clock time such as 8 p.m., and the poster already uses it for the hour.
'For' reports a measured duration, and a concert date is not a length of time.

questions.explanation: Clock times take 'at', full calendar dates take 'on', and a month or a year alone takes 'in', as in 'concert on Saturday 15 March at 8 p.m.'
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The school concert was moved from 6 p.m. ___ 8 p.m. Which preposition marks the new time?
questions.context: English class in Santa Ana, SV.

options.feedback: 'In' introduces a span such as a month or a year, and it cannot mark a new clock time.
A replacement clock time is introduced by 'at', so the concert now takes place at 8 p.m.
'On' goes with days and dates, and the new time here is an hour rather than a calendar day.
'Until' marks the endpoint of a continuing activity, and it does not assign a new starting time.

questions.explanation: When an event is rescheduled to a new clock time, English uses 'at' as in 'moved to 8 p.m.', while 'on' would name a day and 'in' a month or a year.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence reports a duration correctly?
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.text: She has studied English for three years.
options.feedback: 'For' states how long the activity has lasted, and three years is a length of time.

options.text: She has studied English since three years.
options.feedback: 'Since' takes a starting point such as a year or a month, and it cannot be combined with a length.

options.text: She has studied English in three years.
options.feedback: 'In' would place the whole activity inside a closed span and would leave the present situation unstated.

options.text: She has studied English at three years.
options.feedback: 'At' introduces precise clock times, and a length of three years is not an instant of the day.

questions.explanation: 'For' reports a length of time such as three years, while 'since' would name the point where the activity began, and those two prepositions are not interchangeable.

questions.statement: Choose the preposition that completes the sentence: 'The final exam takes place ___ the last week of June.'
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'In' introduces a span of time such as a week, and the last week of June is such a span.
'At' marks a precise instant such as a clock time, and a whole week is not an instant.
'On' goes with a single day or a date, and it does not normally introduce a week.
'For' measures a length the speaker reports, and here the phrase already names the span with 'the last week'.

questions.explanation: A period of time measured in weeks or months takes 'in', so an event placed inside 'the last week of June' is introduced by 'in'.
